text: Decades of research have established the basic contours of the relative age effect. Within age-grouped selection systems, relatively older children may initially demonstrate physical, cognitive, and behavioural advantages that coaches reliably — if mistakenly — interpret as indicators of superior athletic talent [ 10 ], but RAE is best understood as a developmental process in which these initial differences interact with selection decisions and with the opportunities subsequently afforded to selected players [ 7 ]. Children identified early as talented tend to receive more coaching, more deliberate practice, and richer competitive exposure, which can widen the gap between early- and late-born children regardless of the initial talent distribution [ 16 ]. These dynamics are further compounded by coach-expectation effects, differences in confidence and self-efficacy, and self-selection dropout among late-born children who anticipate exclusion [ 3 ]. Meta-analytic reviews confirm that RAEs are pervasive across sports, age groups, and national contexts, and that performance level is among the strongest moderators of effect magnitude: effects tend to be largest where selection is most consequential [ 3 , 4 ].
source_label: Cross-national and historical variation in relative age effects in professional football
